title: Server Basics: Services, Logs and Reverse Proxies
sub: Run servers on your Mac, look inside the request loop, keep services alive with launchd and systemd, read logs, and route requests with nginx
goals: Explain what makes a process a server and choose the right bind address for it
Write and test a JSON API with the standard library, and test application code without a network
Keep a server running with a LaunchAgent on macOS or a systemd unit on Linux, and read its logs
Secure a fresh Linux server in the first fifteen minutes without locking yourself out
Name the failing layer from the symptom a client sees, and predict which nginx location answers a request

blocks.text: Every service you have used in this book so far, from `example.com` to the router admin page to the practice server     inside these pages, is a **server**: an ordinary program that waits on a port and answers whoever connects. Nothing about the     hardware makes something a server. In this chapter you will run servers on your Mac, look inside the request loop that every     web framework hides, learn how Linux and macOS keep a server running after you log out, read server logs like a sysadmin, and     route requests with nginx, the reverse proxy in front of a large share of the web. The next three chapters build on this one:     APIs are what servers offer, encryption is how they protect it, and the cloud is where most of them now run.
What a server really is

A server is a process that asks the kernel for a listening socket on an address and port, then loops: accept a connection,     read a request, write a response, repeat. The client is any process that connects. One machine can run dozens of servers, each on     its own port, and the same program can be a client and a server at once (a web app is a server to browsers and a client of its     database).

blocks.code:
⟪w:CLIENT⟫ (curl, browser, app)                 ⟪w:SERVER⟫ process on 192.168.1.50
───────────────────────────                 ─────────────────────────────────
                                            socket()   make an endpoint
                                            bind()     claim 0.0.0.0:8080
                                            listen()   start the accept queue
connect() ── SYN ───────────────────────▶   ┐
          ◀────────────────── SYN,ACK ──   │ kernel finishes the TCP handshake
          ── ACK ───────────────────────▶   ┘
                                            accept()   take one connection
send("GET /health …") ──────────────────▶   recv()     read the request
          ◀──────────── "HTTP/1.1 200" ──   send()     write the response
close()                                     close()    then back to accept()

blocks.text: Three numbers identify the server's side: the **address** it binds to, the **port** and the **protocol** (TCP or UDP). The     address decides who can reach it, and getting it wrong is the most common way a "private" test server ends up visible to a whole     café Wi-Fi.

blocks.text: When a program binds to an address other than loopback, macOS can show "Do you want the application Python to     accept incoming network connections?". That dialog is the application firewall (System Settings, Network, Firewall). Allow it only     for servers you mean to share. Binding to `127.0.0.1` never triggers it.
Run a real API on your Mac

Below is a complete JSON API written with nothing but the standard library. It is small enough to read in one sitting and     real enough to show everything a framework does for you: routing on method and path, parsing a request body, choosing a status     code, and writing headers before the body. Save it as `~/lab/api_server.py` (in PyCharm: right-click the `lab` folder, New, Python     File).
Start it in one Terminal tab and leave it running. Its log goes to that tab:
In a second tab, talk to it. This transcript is from a real run; your `Date` and Python version will differ:

blocks.code:
$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/health
{"status": "ok", "uptime": 1}
$ curl -si -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/devices -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name": "nas", "ip": "192.168.1.60"}'
HTTP/1.0 201 Created
Server: labapi/1.0 Python/3.13.18
Date: Mon, 16 Nov 2026 23:29:50 GMT
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 46
Location: /devices/3

{"id": 3, "name": "nas", "ip": "192.168.1.60"}
$ curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/devices -d 'oops'
{"error": "send JSON with name and ip"}
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:8080/devices
501

blocks.text: And the first tab, the server's own log, shows one line per request, including the `DELETE` it does not implement:

blocks.code:
$ python3 api_server.py
labapi listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080
127.0.0.1 - - [16/Nov/2026 23:29:50] "GET /health HTTP/1.1" 200 -
127.0.0.1 - - [16/Nov/2026 23:29:50] "POST /devices HTTP/1.1" 201 -
127.0.0.1 - - [16/Nov/2026 23:29:50] "POST /devices HTTP/1.1" 400 -
127.0.0.1 - - [16/Nov/2026 23:29:50] code 501, message Unsupported method ('DELETE')
127.0.0.1 - - [16/Nov/2026 23:29:50] "DELETE /devices HTTP/1.1" 501 -

items.text: **`501 Not Implemented`** came from the base class: `BaseHTTPRequestHandler` looks for a method named `do_DELETE`, finds none and answers for you.

**`HTTP/1.0`** in the status line is the default `protocol_version` of `BaseHTTPRequestHandler`. It closes the connection after every response, which is simple and slow. Production servers speak HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 and keep connections open.
**The `Server` header** leaks the software and Python version. Real deployments usually hide or shorten it.
**Press** [[⌃C]] in the first tab to stop it. The `KeyboardInterrupt` handler prints `bye` instead of a traceback.

blocks.title: Find the process that owns the port

blocks.text: With the server running, run `lsof -nP -iTCP:8080 -sTCP:LISTEN` in the second tab. You get the command     name, its PID and `127.0.0.1:8080 (LISTEN)`. Start a second copy of the server in a third tab and read the error: `OSError: [Errno 48]     Address already in use`. Only one socket can listen on an address and port at a time. That message, and `lsof` to find the culprit,     will save you hours on real servers.
Inside the request loop: WSGI

`api_server.py` mixes two jobs: speaking HTTP on a socket, and deciding what to answer. Real Python deployments split them. A     **server** (gunicorn, uWSGI, or uvicorn for async code) handles sockets, workers and timeouts. Your **application** is a plain     function with a fixed signature, defined in PEP 3333 and called **WSGI**: it receives a dictionary describing the request and a     function for starting the response, and returns the body as a list of bytes. Flask and Django are WSGI applications underneath.     Because the application is just a function, you can call it without any network at all, which is exactly what the box below does in     your browser.

This is how frameworks test your code without opening ports, and it is how you should test your own servers: keep the     decision logic in a function you can call directly, and keep the socket plumbing thin. On your Mac, `wsgiref.simple_server` can serve     the same `app` for real in two lines: `from wsgiref.simple_server import make_server` and `make_server("127.0.0.1", 8081, app).serve_forever()`.

blocks.title: The usual stack, top to bottom
A WSGI router with 404 and 405

task.text: Write a WSGI application `app(environ, start_response)` that serves two routes. `GET /devices` answers `200 OK` with the JSON list        `[{"id": 1, "name": "router"}]`. `GET /health` answers `200 OK` with `{"status": "ok"}`. Any other method on those two paths answers        `405 Method Not Allowed` with an `Allow: GET` header. Any other path answers `404 Not Found`. Every response must have a        `Content-Type: application/json` header and a JSON body.

hints: Check the path first: a wrong path is a 404 whatever the method is.
`start_response(status, headers)` takes a status string such as `"405 Method Not Allowed"` and a list of `(name, value)` tuples.

why.text: Order matters: a path that does not exist is `404` for every method, and only an existing path can be `405`. The `Allow`        header is required by HTTP for `405` responses, so clients can discover what does work. Returning a list containing one bytes object        is the simplest valid WSGI body.

blocks.starter:
import json

def app(environ, start_response):
    # your code
    start_response("200 OK", [("Content-Type", "application/json")])
    return [b"{}"]
blocks.check:
import json
from wsgiref.util import setup_testing_defaults
def call(m, p):
    env = {"REQUEST_METHOD": m, "PATH_INFO": p}
    setup_testing_defaults(env)
    got = {}
    def sr(status, headers):
        got["s"], got["h"] = status, dict(headers)
    body = b"".join(app(env, sr))
    return got["s"], got["h"], json.loads(body)
s, h, b = call("GET", "/devices")
assert s.startswith("200"), "GET /devices should be 200, got " + s
assert b == [{"id": 1, "name": "router"}], "GET /devices body is wrong: " + repr(b)
assert h.get("Content-Type") == "application/json", "Set Content-Type: application/json"
s, h, b = call("GET", "/health")
assert s.startswith("200") and b == {"status": "ok"}, "GET /health should be 200 with {'status': 'ok'}"
s, h, b = call("DELETE", "/devices")
assert s.startswith("405"), "DELETE /devices should be 405, got " + s
assert h.get("Allow") == "GET", "A 405 needs an Allow: GET header"
s, h, b = call("POST", "/nowhere")
assert s.startswith("404"), "An unknown path is 404 whatever the method, got " + s

blocks.text: Keeping a server running: services

A server you start in a Terminal tab dies when you close the tab, log out or reboot, and nobody restarts it when it crashes.     Real servers run as **services** (also called daemons): the operating system's service manager starts them at boot, restarts them     when they fail, collects their output into a log, and runs them as a dedicated user with only the permissions they need. macOS uses     **launchd**. Almost every Linux server uses **systemd**. They solve the same problem with different files.
On your Mac: a LaunchAgent

A **LaunchAgent** runs as you, while you are logged in. A **LaunchDaemon** runs as root at boot, for every user. For a lab     server an agent is right. The job is described by a property list in `~/Library/LaunchAgents/`. Replace `learner` with your account     name (`whoami` prints it) and check the Python path with `which python3`:

blocks.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
    <key>Label</key>
    <string>lab.api</string>
    <key>ProgramArguments</key>
    <array>
        <string>/opt/homebrew/bin/python3</string>
        <string>/Users/learner/lab/api_server.py</string>
    </array>
    <key>WorkingDirectory</key>
    <string>/Users/learner/lab</string>
    <key>RunAtLoad</key>
    <true/>
    <key>KeepAlive</key>
    <true/>
    <key>StandardOutPath</key>
    <string>/Users/learner/lab/api.log</string>
    <key>StandardErrorPath</key>
    <string>/Users/learner/lab/api.log</string>
</dict>
</plist>

cp lab.api.plist ~/Library/LaunchAgents/
plutil -lint ~/Library/LaunchAgents/lab.api.plist
launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/lab.api.plist
launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/lab.api | grep -E 'state|pid|last exit'
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/health

blocks.text: `KeepAlive` means launchd restarts the process whenever it exits, so `kill` it and watch a new PID appear in `launchctl print`.     To stop it for good, unload it with `launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/lab.api` and delete the plist. `launchd` paths must be absolute:     there is no `~` expansion and no shell `PATH`, which is the cause of most "it works in Terminal but not as a service" problems.

`Bootstrap failed: 5: Input/output error` usually means the job is already loaded (bootout first) or the plist     has an error (run `plutil -lint`). A service that starts and immediately exits loops forever under `KeepAlive`; read the log file you     named in `StandardErrorPath`. Recent macOS versions also show the job under System Settings, General, Login Items & Extensions,     where you can switch it off.
On Linux: a systemd unit

On a Raspberry Pi, a homelab VM or a cloud server, the same service is a **unit file**. Put it in `/etc/systemd/system/labapi.service`.     It runs the app as an unprivileged user, restarts it on failure and sends its output to the journal:

blocks.code:
[Unit]
Description=Lab JSON API
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=labapi
Group=labapi
WorkingDirectory=/opt/labapi
ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 /opt/labapi/api_server.py
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2
NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=true
PrivateTmp=true

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

sudo useradd --system --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin labapi
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now labapi
systemctl status labapi
journalctl -u labapi -f

blocks.text: The `Protect…` and `NoNewPrivileges` lines are systemd's sandboxing: the service sees the filesystem read-only, cannot read     home directories and cannot gain privileges through setuid programs. They cost one line each and limit what an attacker gets if the     app is ever compromised. `systemd-analyze security labapi` scores a unit and lists what else you could lock down.

blocks.title: The same tasks on both systems

blocks.name: systemctl
blocks.sum: Start, stop, enable, inspect and restart systemd services on a Linux machine.

how.text: `systemctl` talks to systemd, process 1 on almost every current Linux distribution. A **unit** is anything systemd manages: a service, a timer, a mount, a socket. `start` and `stop` act now; `enable` and `disable` decide what happens at the next boot by creating or removing links from a target such as `multi-user.target`. `enable --now` does both.

Changing a unit file does nothing until `daemon-reload`, which makes systemd re-read every unit. `restart` stops and starts the service; `reload` asks it to re-read its own configuration without dropping connections, if the service supports that (nginx does).

flags.d: state, PID, memory, the command line and the last ten log lines
start it and start it at every boot
full restart, or re-read the configuration in place
re-read unit files after you edit them
list units that failed
print the unit file and any drop-in overrides
create an override file instead of editing the vendor unit

examples.desc: Check a service and its recent log lines
Start a service now and at every boot
List the names of every failed unit

gotchas: `systemctl status` uses a pager. Add `--no-pager` in scripts, or the script waits for you to press q.
Editing `/lib/systemd/system/*.service` directly is lost on the next package update. Use `systemctl edit NAME` to create an override.

blocks.name: journalctl
blocks.sum: Read and follow the systemd journal: the log of the kernel, every service and the boot.
blocks.syntax: journalctl [-u UNIT] [-f] [--since TIME] [-p PRIORITY] [-n N] [-o FORMAT]

how.text: systemd captures everything a service writes to stdout and stderr, adds metadata (unit, PID, priority, boot ID, timestamp) and stores it in a binary journal. `journalctl` queries it. Filters combine, so `-u nginx -p err --since today` means errors from nginx today.
On many distributions the journal is kept only in memory until `/var/log/journal` exists. Create that directory (or set `Storage=persistent`) if you want logs to survive a reboot.

flags.d: one service (repeatable)
follow new lines, like `tail -f`
time filter; also `--until`, `today`, `yesterday`, full timestamps
priority `err` and worse (emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug)
this boot only; `-b -1` for the previous boot
last 50 lines
one JSON object per line, for scripts

examples.desc: Count log lines per service in the last hour
examples.code: journalctl --since '1 hour ago' -o json | jq -r '._SYSTEMD_UNIT // "kernel"' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

gotchas: Without `sudo` (or membership of the `systemd-journal` or `adm` group) you may see only your own user's messages and a hint about missing permissions.

blocks.name: launchctl bootstrap
blocks.sum: Load, unload, restart and inspect a launchd service with the modern domain-target subcommands.

how.text: launchd is process 1 on macOS. Every job lives in a **domain**: `gui/501` for agents of the logged-in user with UID 501, `system` for daemons. The modern subcommands take a domain target: `bootstrap gui/$(id -u) FILE` loads a plist, `bootout gui/$(id -u)/LABEL` unloads it, `print` dumps its state, and `kickstart -k` restarts it.
The older `load` and `unload` subcommands still work, but Apple documents them as legacy and their error messages are less useful.

flags.d: load a LaunchAgent for the current user
stop and unload it
state, PID, last exit code, program, environment
kill and restart the running job
every job in your domain with PID and last exit status

examples.desc: Load your lab API as a LaunchAgent
Restart it after changing the script

gotchas: Paths in a plist must be absolute, and the job does not inherit your shell's `PATH`. Call programs by full path such as `/opt/homebrew/bin/python3`.
Editing a loaded plist changes nothing until you `bootout` and `bootstrap` it again.

blocks.name: ss
blocks.sum: List sockets on Linux: who is listening on which port, and every open connection.

how.text: `ss` reads socket state straight from the kernel through netlink, which makes it fast even on busy servers. It replaced `netstat` on Linux. The macOS equivalent for "who listens on this port" is `lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN`.

The `Local Address:Port` column tells you the bind address. `0.0.0.0:80` or `*:80` is open on every interface; `127.0.0.1:5432` is loopback only. That one column answers "can the network reach this?" before you even touch the firewall.

flags.d: TCP / UDP sockets
listening sockets only
numbers, no name lookups
the owning process (needs `sudo` for other users' processes)
filter by state

examples.desc: Every listening TCP port and the program behind it
Count established connections per remote address
examples.code: ss -tn state established | awk 'NR > 1 {split($4, a, ":"); print a[1]}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

blocks.text: Reading server logs

Logs are a server's memory. When something breaks, the first question is always "what does the log say?", and the second is     "what changed?". The most common format on the web is the **combined log format**, written by nginx and Apache for every request:

blocks.title: One line of an nginx access log

tokens.exp: client address (or the proxy's, unless you configure real-IP headers)
identity and authenticated user: almost always empty
when the request finished, with the server's UTC offset
the request line: method, path with query string, protocol
the status code the server sent
response body size in bytes, not counting headers
the Referer header: the page that linked here
the User-Agent header: what the client says it is

blocks.text: The box below parses a small log with one regular expression and answers the three questions you ask every time: how much traffic, how many errors, and what is failing.

blocks.code:
import re
from collections import Counter

LOG = """203.0.113.50 - - [16/Nov/2026:10:02:11 +0000] "GET /api/devices HTTP/2.0" 200 412 "-" "curl/8.7.1"
198.51.100.7 - - [16/Nov/2026:10:02:12 +0000] "GET / HTTP/2.0" 200 1530 "-" "Mozilla/5.0"
198.51.100.7 - - [16/Nov/2026:10:02:12 +0000] "GET /static/app.css HTTP/2.0" 200 8812 "https://app.lab.example/" "Mozilla/5.0"
192.0.2.66 - - [16/Nov/2026:10:02:13 +0000] "GET /wp-login.php HTTP/1.1" 404 153 "-" "python-requests/2.32"
192.0.2.66 - - [16/Nov/2026:10:02:13 +0000] "GET /.env HTTP/1.1" 404 153 "-" "python-requests/2.32"
203.0.113.50 - - [16/Nov/2026:10:02:15 +0000] "POST /api/devices HTTP/2.0" 502 157 "-" "curl/8.7.1"
203.0.113.50 - - [16/Nov/2026:10:02:19 +0000] "POST /api/devices HTTP/2.0" 502 157 "-" "curl/8.7.1"
198.51.100.7 - - [16/Nov/2026:10:02:21 +0000] "GET /api/devices HTTP/2.0" 200 412 "-" "Mozilla/5.0"
"""

LINE = re.compile(r'(\S+) \S+ \S+ \[([^\]]+)\] "(\S+) (\S+) [^"]*" (\d{3}) (\d+)')
rows = [LINE.match(l).groups() for l in LOG.strip().splitlines()]

print(len(rows), "requests,", sum(int(r[5]) for r in rows), "bytes")
print("by status:", dict(sorted(Counter(r[4][0] + "xx" for r in rows).items())))
errors = Counter((r[2], r[3], r[4]) for r in rows if r[4] >= "500")
for (method, path, status), n in errors.most_common():
    print("server error:", n, "x", method, path, status)
probes = sorted({r[0] for r in rows if r[4] == "404"})
print("404s came from:", ", ".join(probes))
blocks.out:
8 requests, 11786 bytes
by status: {'2xx': 4, '4xx': 2, '5xx': 2}
server error: 2 x POST /api/devices 502
404s came from: 192.0.2.66

blocks.text: Two patterns show up in almost every real log. The `502` lines are your problem: the proxy could not reach the application.     The `404`s for `/wp-login.php` and `/.env` are not: automated scanners request well-known files on every public IP address all day.     They are noise, but they also prove your server is visible to the whole internet within minutes of going live.

On a real server the same questions are one pipeline each:     `awk '{print $9}' /var/log/nginx/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` counts status codes, and     `awk '$9 >= 500 {print $7}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head` lists the paths that fail. Field 9 is the status and     field 7 the path, because `awk` splits on spaces and the date contains one.

blocks.title: Error rate per path

task.text: Write `error_rates(lines)` that takes access-log lines in the combined format and returns a dictionary mapping each path to the        fraction of its requests that got a status of 500 or higher, rounded to two decimal places. Ignore the query string, so        `/api/devices?type=pi` counts as `/api/devices`. Paths with no errors map to `0.0`.

hints: `re.search(r'"\S+ (\S+) [^"]*" (\d{3}) ', line)` captures the path and the status.
Count totals and errors in two dictionaries, then divide.

why.text: Error *rate* per path beats a raw count: ten errors out of ten requests is an outage, ten out of a million is noise. Splitting        on `?` groups the same endpoint with different parameters, which is what you want when the question is "which endpoint is broken".

blocks.check:
L = ['1.1.1.1 - - [x] "GET /a?x=1 HTTP/1.1" 200 5 "-" "c"', '1.1.1.1 - - [x] "GET /a HTTP/1.1" 502 5 "-" "c"',
     '1.1.1.1 - - [x] "POST /b HTTP/1.1" 201 5 "-" "c"', '1.1.1.1 - - [x] "GET /a HTTP/1.1" 200 5 "-" "c"',
     '1.1.1.1 - - [x] "GET /c HTTP/1.1" 503 5 "-" "c"', 'garbage line']
r = error_rates(L)
assert isinstance(r, dict), "Return a dict"
assert r.get("/a") == 0.33, "/a had 1 error in 3 requests: expected 0.33, got " + repr(r.get("/a"))
assert r.get("/b") == 0.0, "/b had no errors: expected 0.0"
assert r.get("/c") == 1.0, "/c failed every time: expected 1.0"
assert "/a?x=1" not in r, "Ignore the query string"

blocks.text: A Linux server in its first fifteen minutes

Sooner or later your server runs on Linux: a Raspberry Pi on your shelf, a VM in your homelab or a small cloud instance.     You will reach it with `ssh` (the SSH chapter covers keys and config). These are the first things to do on a fresh Debian or Ubuntu     machine, in order. Each one closes a door that automated attacks try within hours.

items.text: **Update everything**: `sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y`, then reboot if the kernel changed.
**Create your own user** and stop using `root` or a default account: `sudo adduser learner` then `sudo usermod -aG sudo learner`.
**Install your SSH key** for that user from your Mac: `ssh-copy-id learner@{{ip}}`, then log in once with the key to prove it works.

**Turn off password logins**: in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` (or a file in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/`) set `PasswordAuthentication no` and `PermitRootLogin no`, check with `sudo sshd -t`, then `sudo systemctl reload ssh`. Keep your current session open until a new login works.
**Turn on a firewall** that allows only what you serve: `sudo ufw allow OpenSSH`, `sudo ufw allow 443/tcp`, `sudo ufw enable`.
**Install security updates automatically**: `sudo apt install unattended-upgrades` and confirm `/etc/apt/apt.conf.d/20auto-upgrades` enables them.
**Set the time zone and check the clock**: `timedatectl`. TLS certificates, logs and two-factor codes all depend on a correct clock.

blocks.text: Changing SSH or firewall settings over SSH is the classic way to lose a server. Always allow SSH in the     firewall *before* `ufw enable`, test a new login in a second Terminal tab *before* closing the first, and know your way back in: a     monitor and keyboard for a Pi, or the provider's web console for a cloud machine.

blocks.name: ufw
blocks.sum: Uncomplicated Firewall: a friendly front end to the Linux packet filter for Debian and Ubuntu.

how.text: ufw writes nftables or iptables rules for you. Its default policy, once enabled, is to deny incoming connections and allow outgoing ones, so you only describe what should be reachable. Rules can name a port (`443/tcp`), an application profile that a package installed (`OpenSSH`, `Nginx Full`) or a source network (`from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 22`).
A firewall rule stops packets before any program sees them. The client sees a timeout, not a refusal, which is how you tell "blocked" from "nothing listening" when you troubleshoot.

flags.d: open a port to everyone
open a port to one network only
list rules with numbers
remove rule number N
turn the firewall on or off (enable persists across reboots)
application profiles installed by packages

examples.desc: Allow SSH from your LAN only, then HTTPS from anywhere
examples.code:
sudo ufw allow from {{subnet}} to any port 22 proto tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
sudo ufw enable

gotchas: Docker publishes container ports by writing its own iptables rules, which bypass ufw. A port published with `-p 8080:80` can be reachable even when ufw says it is closed. Publish to `127.0.0.1:8080:80` instead, or use your cloud firewall.

blocks.text: A request's journey through a server

Production servers are a stack, not a program. A request to a typical web app passes through DNS, a firewall, a reverse proxy     that terminates TLS, an application server and a database, and each layer fails in its own recognisable way. Learn the symptoms and     you can point at the broken layer from your laptop, before you even log in.

blocks.title: Symptom to layer
Name the broken layer

task.text: For each report, name the layer that is most likely broken and the first command you would run: (a) "The site loaded yesterday;        today the browser says the connection is not private and the certificate expired." (b) "curl hangs for over a minute and then fails."        (c) "We get a page from nginx that says 502 Bad Gateway." (d) "curl prints Connection refused immediately."

hints: A timeout means nobody answered. A refusal means the machine answered "no one here".
A 5xx status means an HTTP server answered, so DNS, the network and TLS all worked.
blocks.solution:
(a) TLS: the certificate on the proxy expired. Run openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST and read notAfter; renew (certbot renew) and reload nginx.
(b) Network or firewall: packets are being dropped. Run nc -vz -w 3 HOST 443 and check the firewall or cloud security group, and whether the machine is running at all.
(c) The application behind nginx: nginx is fine but cannot reach its upstream. On the server: systemctl status APP, then the nginx error log (connect() failed ... while connecting to upstream).
(d) The server machine is reachable but nothing listens on that port: the proxy or service is stopped. On the server: sudo ss -ltnp and systemctl status nginx.

why.text: The kind of failure carries information. Errors that arrive instantly come from a machine that received your packet; errors        after a long wait come from silence. An HTTP status code proves every layer below HTTP is healthy. Reading symptoms this way lets        you skip whole layers when you troubleshoot.

blocks.text: Reverse proxies and nginx

Almost no application faces the internet directly. A **reverse proxy** sits in front: it accepts every connection, handles     TLS, serves static files fast, applies limits, and forwards the rest to one or more applications on private ports. It means your     Python or Node process never has to cope with slow clients, certificate renewals or a flood of connections. nginx is the most common     one; Caddy is a newer, simpler alternative that obtains HTTPS certificates automatically.

blocks.code:
⟪c:internet⟫                     ⟪w:one server⟫
browser ──https──▶ :443 ⟪b:nginx⟫ ──┬── /api/*     ──http──▶ 127.0.0.1:8000  ⟪y:Python app⟫
curl    ──https──▶       TLS     ├── /static/*  ──────────▶ /srv/www        ⟪d:files on disk⟫
phone   ──https──▶       limits  └── /          ──http──▶ 127.0.0.1:3000  ⟪y:Node front end⟫
                                  only :443 is open; the apps listen on loopback

blocks.text: A small but complete site configuration looks like this. It lives in `/etc/nginx/sites-available/` on Debian and Ubuntu (linked into `sites-enabled/`), or in `/etc/nginx/conf.d/*.conf` elsewhere:

items.text: **`proxy_set_header`** lines pass on what the proxy knows and the app does not: the original host name, the client's address and whether the request came over HTTPS. Without them every request looks as if it came from `127.0.0.1` over plain HTTP.
**`proxy_read_timeout`** is how long nginx waits for the app to start answering. When it runs out, the client gets the `504` you met above. The default is 60 seconds.
**`client_max_body_size`** caps uploads (default 1 MB). A bigger upload gets a `413` error page from nginx before your app sees it.

blocks.text: The question people get wrong most often is which `location` handles a request. nginx does **not** take the first match in the     file. Exact matches (`=`) win outright, then the longest matching prefix is remembered, then regular expressions are tried in order,     and a regex match beats the remembered prefix unless that prefix was marked `^~`. Work through the examples below until you can predict     every answer, then edit the config and try to break your own predictions.

`location /admin` also matches `/administrator` and `/admin-old.zip`: a prefix is compared character by character, not     path segment by path segment. Write `location /admin/` (with the slash) when you mean the directory, and remember that `/admin` itself then     falls through to another block.

blocks.name: nginx -t
blocks.sum: Test the nginx configuration for errors before you reload it, and print the merged config.

how.text: `-t` parses every configuration file, checks syntax and that referenced files such as certificates exist, and reports the first problem with its file and line. It does not touch the running server.
`-T` does the same and then prints the entire merged configuration, every `include` expanded, which is the fastest way to answer "what is nginx actually running with?".

The safe change routine is always the same: edit, `sudo nginx -t`, and only then `sudo systemctl reload nginx`. A reload starts new worker processes with the new configuration and lets old ones finish their requests, so nobody is disconnected. If the test fails, the running server is untouched.

flags.d: test the configuration and exit
test, then dump the full configuration
signal the running master to reload (the same as `systemctl reload nginx`)

examples.code: sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx

examples.desc: List every server_name nginx knows about

gotchas: `systemctl restart nginx` with a broken config stops the old server and fails to start the new one: an outage. `reload` with a broken config keeps the old one running.

questions.q: A test server bound to `0.0.0.0:8000` on your laptop. Who can connect?

options.text: Anything that can reach any of the laptop's interfaces, unless a firewall blocks it
Nobody until you open the port in the router

questions.why: `0.0.0.0` means every interface: loopback, Wi-Fi, Ethernet, VPN. Your router's NAT usually keeps the internet out, but everyone on the same network can connect. Bind to `127.0.0.1` for private work.

questions.q: Starting a second copy of a server fails with `Address already in use`. Why?

options.text: Another socket is already listening on that address and port

questions.why: Only one listening socket can own an address and port. Find the owner with `lsof -nP -iTCP:PORT -sTCP:LISTEN` on macOS or `sudo ss -ltnp` on Linux.

questions.q: Which file makes macOS keep your script running and restart it when it crashes?
questions.why: launchd runs jobs described by plists; `KeepAlive` restarts them on exit. systemd units are the Linux equivalent.

questions.q: Users see `502 Bad Gateway` from nginx. What do you know?

options.text: nginx is running but could not get a response from its upstream application

questions.why: A 502 is generated by the proxy itself, so DNS, the network, TLS and nginx all worked. The application behind it is down, crashed or listening somewhere else.

options.text: `location ~* \.json$`, because a regex match beats a plain prefix

questions.why: nginx remembers the longest prefix (`/api/`), then tries regexes. The regex matches, so it wins. Adding `^~` to the prefix would stop the regex check.

questions.q: Why put a reverse proxy in front of an application server?

options.text: It makes the application code run faster
It handles TLS, static files, limits and slow clients so the app only sees clean requests on a private port

questions.why: The proxy is the hardened front door. The app listens on loopback and never touches certificates or raw internet traffic.

blocks.title: status: a supervised service with a health check

blocks.text: Turn `api_server.py` into something you would be happy to leave running: a service that starts at login, restarts when it dies,             logs in a format you can parse, and exposes a health check that a monitor can poll. The API client you write in the next chapter             talks to this server, so keep it.
1. Add structured logging

Override `log_message` in the handler so every request is logged as one JSON object per line with the time, client, method,             path, status and duration in milliseconds. JSON lines are easy to filter with `jq` and to ship to a log system later. Record the             start time in `parse_request` (call the parent first) and compute the duration in `log_request`.
2. Make the health check honest

`/health` should report `ok` only if the service can do its job. Add a check that the data file it writes to is writable and             return `503` with `{"status": "degraded", "reason": "…"}` when it is not. A health check that always says ok is worse than none.
3. Supervise it with launchd

Install the LaunchAgent from this chapter, point `StandardErrorPath` at `~/lab/api.log`, and prove `KeepAlive` works:             find the PID, `kill` it, and run `launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/lab.api` until a new PID appears.
4. Watch it
Write `~/lab/watch_api.zsh`, a loop that polls `/health` every five seconds and prints a timestamped line only when the status changes:

blocks.code:
#!/bin/zsh
# watch_api.zsh - print a line whenever the health status changes
url=${1:-http://127.0.0.1:8080/health}
last=""
while true; do
  code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 3 "$url")
  if [[ $code != "$last" ]]; then
    print "$(date '+%H:%M:%S') health=$code"
    last=$code
  fi
  sleep 5
done

items.text: Count requests per status code in memory and serve them at `/metrics` as plain text, one `name value` pair per line.
Run the same script on a Raspberry Pi or Linux VM as the systemd unit from this chapter, behind nginx.
Make `watch_api.zsh` send a macOS notification on change with `osascript -e 'display notification "health changed" with title "lab api"'`.

terms.def: a process that listens on an address and port and answers requests from clients
the local address a listening socket accepts connections on: 127.0.0.1 for this machine only, 0.0.0.0 for every interface
a long-running background process, usually started and supervised by the service manager
the macOS service manager and process 1; runs LaunchAgents and LaunchDaemons from plists
the Linux service manager and process 1 on most distributions; runs units such as services and timers
the Python standard interface (PEP 3333) between a web server and an application function
a server that accepts client connections and forwards requests to applications behind it
in nginx, the application server a request is forwarded to
status sent by a proxy when it cannot get a valid response from the upstream
status sent by a proxy when the upstream does not answer in time
one line per request: client, time, request line, status, size, referrer and user agent
